BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a build_chapter_map card:
- card.parts group the chapter's items by content type; card.coverage.must_cover lists every teachable item: each must be in the item_ids
  of at least one concept.
- The source lines are "item id | page | kind | type | teachable | exam | content | prerequisites".
How to fill the JSON:
- concepts: group the items into the chapter's concepts; every teachable item belongs to at least one concept (use the item ids exactly
  as given); content_type is the concept's main type (one of BIE's nine ids, never "none": a concept of practice or PYQ questions takes
  the type of what its questions test); core_explanation says the concept's heart in two or three sentences a teacher would say.
- relations: how concepts relate, using concept ids. "A depends_on B" means B must be understood first; "A causes B"; "A sequence_next B"
  means A comes before B in time or in a process. BIE's code checks with its prerequisite and reasoning engines: prerequisites never go
  in a circle, the teaching order teaches a prerequisite before what needs it, cause and effect never go in a circle, and dated concepts
  never go back in time.
- prerequisites_to_teach: only what this chapter directly needs, never a prerequisite of a prerequisite (no chains), each with why it
  is needed and needed_for = the chapter concept ids that need it. BIE teaches them in one short video before the chapter (S1-12, S2-03).
  Usually that is 8 or fewer; never drop a prerequisite the chapter directly needs to stay under 8.
- prerequisite_note: "" when there are 8 or fewer prerequisites; with more than 8, why every one of them is directly needed (BIE's code
  asks for this note; it is a warning, not a limit).
- cross_references: every reference such as "Fig. 6.10" or "see table" resolved to the item it means.
- question_links: every question item (a question "continued from the previous page" too) linked to the concepts it tests; link the
  question item, never its answer options.
- teaching_order: every concept id exactly once, in the order a teacher should teach them, starting from what the student knows.
- exam_focus: the concepts most important for this exam and why.

output.chapter_summary: Cells form tissues that divide work and build organs, organ systems and organisms. The chapter compares cell division, classifies animal and plant tissues, relates their microscopic structure to location and function, and tests recognition through diagrams, comparisons and multiple-choice questions.

concepts.name: Tissues, division of labour and levels of organisation
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Cells combining to perform the same function form a tissue; plant cells form plant tissues and animal cells form animal tissues. Grouping work into tissues produces division of labour, reduces the workload on individual cells and supports organisation into Cell → Tissues → Organ → Organ system → Organisms. Read these arrows as component-to-larger-whole relationships, not as stages in one cell's life.

concepts.name: Mitosis versus meiosis
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Mitosis is compared with meiosis by somatic versus germ-cell occurrence, one versus two nuclear divisions, two versus four daughter cells, diploid versus haploid products, greater versus lesser frequency, somatic-organ versus gamete formation, one versus two sets of division phases, and five subphases of meiotic prophase I. It contrasts chromosome-number maintenance with halving, absence with presence of crossing over, and equational with reduction division; its additional chromosome-doubling row says doubling occurs at the start of mitosis but after the first meiotic division in meiosis. Outside correction: DNA replicates before mitosis and before meiosis I, not between meiosis I and II; replication doubles DNA content rather than chromosome number counted by centromeres, and meiosis II is equational.

concepts.name: Plant versus animal mitosis
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Plant mitosis is presented as lacking centrioles and asters, dividing the cytoplasm through a cell plate, and occurring mainly at meristems; animal mitosis has centrioles and asters, cytoplasmic furrowing and cleavage, and distribution through body tissues. Outside clarification: This is the usual higher-plant versus animal comparison rather than an exception-free rule for all plants or all animal cells; a cell plate builds a separating partition, whereas cleavage constricts the animal cell.

concepts.name: Animal-tissue classification and functional overview
concepts.core_explanation: Book: The four animal-tissue groups are epithelial for covering or lining, muscular for movement, neural for responding to stimuli, and connective for supporting, linking and cushioning. The tree divides epithelium into simple squamous, stratified squamous, columnar, ciliated columnar, cuboidal and glandular forms, and muscle into striated, non-striated and cardiac forms. Connective tissue branches into connective tissue proper—areolar, adipose and fibrous—supportive tissue—cartilage and bone—and fluid tissue—blood and lymph; neural tissue has no further branch shown.

concepts.name: Animal tissues located in the human body
concepts.core_explanation: Book figure: Connect the body to cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle cells; nerve tissue and nerve cells associated with brain, spinal cord and nerves; and epithelial linings of the gastrointestinal tract and other hollow organs. Recognise ciliated columnar, simple columnar, simple cuboidal and simple squamous drawings, and distinguish the skin surface from the basement membrane beneath its epithelial layers. The connective panel identifies tendon, bone, fat cells, and fat and other soft padding tissue; its pointers locate examples rather than show a process.

concepts.name: Epithelial sheets, barriers and gland formation
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Epithelium covers most organs and cavities, forming a continuous sheet of tightly packed cells with little cementing material and almost no intercellular spaces; an extracellular fibrous basement membrane usually separates it from underlying tissue. This arrangement forms a barrier between body systems. Epithelial cells may specialise into surface-secreting gland cells, and inward folding of an epithelial portion can form a multicellular gland called glandular epithelium.

concepts.name: Epithelial types: shape, layers, locations and functions
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Simple squamous is a single flat, irregular-boundaried layer in blood vessels, capillaries, lung air sacs and Bowman's capsule for diffusion with minimal protection; simple cuboidal lines kidney tubules and gland ducts for absorption and secretion, with microvilli mentioned in proximal convoluted tubules; simple columnar is tall and slender, often ciliated, in digestive and upper respiratory linings for protection, absorption, mucus secretion and directional movement. Stratified squamous protects mouth and vagina through renewed layers whose older cells flatten above an active columnar basal layer; stratified cuboidal protects mammary, sweat and salivary gland ducts; stratified columnar protects and secretes in the male urethra and lobar salivary ducts; pseudostratified columnar has unequal cell heights in respiratory passages and gland ducts for protection, secretion and mucus movement. Keratinised outer cells are described as dead and lacking nucleus and cytoplasm, with keratin providing waterproofing and abrasion protection; transitional urothelium in bladder, urethra and ureter changes from cuboidal-looking to flattened irregular cells during stretching, accommodating liquid volume and forming a tight-junction barrier—outside clarification: cuboidal cells are approximately cube-shaped, pseudostratification is apparent rather than true layering, and urothelium lines only part of the urethra.

concepts.name: Recognising epithelial tissues in drawings
concepts.core_explanation: Book figures: Identify squamous by flat cells, cuboidal by approximately equal cell height and width, columnar by tall cells, and ciliated columnar by projections on the free surface. Compare simple single layers with stratified squamous and stratified cuboidal blocks, then recognise pseudostratified columnar by nuclei at differing heights and transitional epithelium by rounded superficial cells above underlying layers. Fig. 6.9 and the seven-block comparison show parallel tissue forms, not a transformation sequence.

concepts.name: Connective tissue: matrix, fibres and mechanical properties
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Connective tissue supports, joins, binds and packs body parts, helping prevent organ displacement during movement; relatively few loosely spaced cells lie within an intercellular matrix that may be jelly-like, fluid, dense or rigid. Cells secrete a polysaccharide gel and protein fibres: widespread collagen is flexible with high tensile strength, elastin forms stretchable networks that recoil, and thin reticulate fibres containing collagen and glycoproteins form delicate networks joining neighbouring tissues. In the diagram, distinguish ground substance and collagen grouped as extracellular matrix from mesenchymal cells, macrophage and adipocytes, and identify thick collagen fibres, finer elastic fibres and the blood vessel.

concepts.name: Connective-tissue varieties, locations and functions
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Loose connective tissue supports and provides elasticity in deep skin layers and around vessels, nerves and organs; dense tissue in tendons and ligaments strongly packs structures together; elastic tissue supplies elasticity in lungs, arteries, trachea and vocal cords. Specialised cartilage at long-bone ends, nose tip, larynx and trachea provides flexible support, bone protects and supports muscle attachment, and vascular connective tissue within vessels transports oxygen and carbon dioxide and participates in immunity and clotting. Adipose tissue in deep skin, around the heart and kidneys, and around joints provides support, protection, heat conservation and an energy source.

concepts.name: Connective-tissue visual atlas
concepts.core_explanation: Book Fig. 6.10: Identify white blood corpuscles and their cytoplasm and nuclei—neutrophil or polymorphonuclear leucocyte, eosinophil, basophil, lymphocyte and monocyte—alongside platelets and a red blood corpuscle. Compact bone shows concentric arrangements around Haversian canals containing blood vessels and nerve fibres, with canaliculi containing slender osteocyte processes; hyaline cartilage shows chondrocytes in hyaline matrix. Areolar tissue labels reticular fibre, fibroblast, macrophage, collagen fibre, mast cell and plasma cell, while adipose tissue labels adipocytes, large fat droplets and peripheral nuclei; these are separate examples rather than steps.

concepts.name: Muscle fibres and contraction
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Muscular tissue consists of large elongated muscle cells, also called muscle fibres, containing contractile proteins and carrying out contraction and relaxation. Its three types are skeletal, smooth and cardiac. Outside explanation: Contraction generates tension or shortening, and relaxation reduces active tension; a muscle fibre is a cell, unlike a secreted collagen or elastic fibre in connective tissue.

concepts.name: Skeletal muscle: movement and posture
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Skeletal muscle has elongated cylindrical, unbranched fibres attached to bones, with many nuclei and alternating dark and light bands called striations. It helps body movement and posture, is described as easily fatigued, and is also called striated or voluntary muscle. The banded fibre bundle beside the bent arm connects microscopic appearance to its bone-moving role.

concepts.name: Smooth or visceral muscle
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Smooth fibres are unbranched spindle-shaped or fusiform cells with tapering ends, one central nucleus and no striations; they are also called unstriated or involuntary muscles. Examples include stomach, intestine, eye and blood vessels, and the function highlighted is peristalsis; the intestine-linked drawing shows the same spindle cells without transverse bands. The book says they do not fatigue—outside clarification: this expresses their resistance to fatigue in sustained normal activity, and peristalsis is coordinated contraction and relaxation that propels contents along a hollow organ.

concepts.name: Cardiac muscle
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Cardiac muscle consists of cylindrical, branched, striated fibres, each described as uninucleate, and is involuntary. Contraction and relaxation of the heart wall pump and distribute blood, and the paired tissue-and-heart illustration links branching striped fibres to this location. The book says cardiac muscle does not fatigue—outside clarification: it is highly fatigue-resistant under normal conditions, rather than incapable of functional failure.

concepts.name: Comparing skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Skeletal muscle lies at the skeleton, produces movement, heat and posture, and has parallel striated fibres with multiple eccentric nuclei under voluntary control; cardiac muscle lies in the heart, pumps continuously, and is striated with one central nucleus under involuntary control. Visceral smooth muscle occurs in the gastrointestinal tract, uterus, eye and blood vessels, has one central nucleus without striations, and acts involuntarily in peristalsis, blood-pressure regulation, pupil size and hair erection. The three drawings distinguish a long unbranched multinucleate cylinder, branching striped cardiac fibres, and a tapered smooth cell; striation and voluntary control must therefore be treated as different criteria.

concepts.name: Neuron structure and direction of impulse transmission
concepts.core_explanation: Book question: 'How do neurons transmit impulses (send message to other cells)?'; the diagram shows an incoming axon of a previous neuron approaching a synapse, the receiving neuron's dendritic and cell-body region with nucleus, an electrical signal travelling along its axon, and axon tips meeting the next neuron's dendrites at another synapse. Follow the indicated direction toward the next cell, identifying dendrites, cell body, axon and terminal tips rather than treating connected cells as one continuous cell. Outside explanation: At a typical chemical synapse, transmitter released from the axon terminal crosses a small gap and affects the receiving cell; the supplied diagram itself does not describe this chemical mechanism.

concepts.name: Plant-tissue classification
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Plant tissues branch into meristematic—apical, lateral and intercalary—and permanent—simple and complex; simple permanent tissues are parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma, with aerenchyma and chlorenchyma under parenchyma and fibres and sclereids under sclerenchyma. Complex permanent tissues are xylem and phloem: the visible page-1 entries list tracheids, vessels or tracheae and xylem parenchyma under xylem, and sieve tubes, companion cells and phloem parenchyma under phloem. The page-1 component lists meet a crop edge, so use later explicit component descriptions to complete them rather than assuming that the visible lists are exhaustive.

concepts.name: Meristematic cells and locations of plant growth
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Meristematic tissue occurs in growing root and shoot regions; its highly active dividing cells are spherical, oval or rectangular, compactly packed without intercellular spaces, and described as lacking vacuoles. Apical meristems at root and shoot tips increase length, lateral meristems beneath bark increase root or stem girth, and intercalary meristems at leaf or internode bases increase organ length. Read the shoot, root, stem and node insets and repeated position diagrams together: blue arrows mark lengthwise growth, orange arrows mark outward thickening, and leader lines merely identify locations; the source's 'nodes' wording for elongation is understood as internodes.

concepts.name: Differentiation and permanent tissue
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Differentiation is the process of taking up a permanent shape, size and function; permanent tissue is described as losing the ability to divide and adopting a specific role. The general notes list a large central vacuole, a thick cell wall, and roles in protection, support, storage and photosynthesis. Book qualification from later pages: parenchyma has thin walls and mature sclerenchyma lacks living contents, so these general features should not be applied uniformly to every permanent-tissue cell.

concepts.name: Simple permanent tissue and parenchyma specialisations
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Simple permanent tissue contains one structurally and functionally similar cell type; its introductory functions include food storage and photosynthesis. Parenchyma occurs in stems, roots, leaves, flowers and fruits, with thin-walled round, polygonal or elongated cells separated by intercellular spaces, and acts as food-storage tissue. Chlorophyll-containing parenchyma is chlorenchyma, while aerenchyma has loosely arranged cells and air spaces that provide buoyancy and help plant parts float.

concepts.name: Collenchyma: flexible mechanical support
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Collenchyma occurs in leaf stalks and dicot stems and consists of living elongated cells with irregular corner thickening and very little intercellular space. It supplies mechanical strength while permitting flexibility and bending, with photosynthesis also listed among its functions. Tendrils and climber stems illustrate why support must sometimes resist pulling without making a growing organ rigid.

concepts.name: Sclerenchyma: lignified strength and protection
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Sclerenchyma occurs around stem vascular bundles, in leaf veins and hard seed and nut coverings, with coconut husk as an example; its dead cells lack intercellular spaces and have thick lignified walls that provide strength and protection. The prose describes long narrow cells and says excessive thickening makes the cavity absent, while the chapter's figures also show stone cells and a lumen. Outside clarification: fibres and sclereids differ in shape, and lignified walls generally leave a narrow lumen rather than requiring its complete absence.

concepts.name: Comparative anatomy of the three simple permanent tissues
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Compare parenchyma's oval, spherical or polygonal isodiametric cells and thin cellulosic primary walls, collenchyma's circular, oval or polyhedral profiles and uneven primary-wall thickening, and sclerenchyma's variable fibres and sclereids with thick lignified secondary walls; the first two retain cytoplasm, nuclei and vacuoles, whereas mature sclerenchyma lacks these, and spaces are present in parenchyma but absent or very small in the others. The table locates parenchyma in soft packing parts, pith, cortex and medullary rays; collenchyma in dicot stems, petioles and beneath epidermis, described as absent in monocots and roots; and sclerenchyma in dicot hypodermis, bundle sheath, pericycle, seeds and fruit pulp, linking storage/photosynthesis, tensile flexible support, and stress-resistant protection respectively. In the diagrams distinguish lengthwise and cross-sectional views, thin primary walls, uneven thickening, thick secondary walls, fibre, stone cell and lumen; the label 'intracellular spaces' actually points between cells, and the sclerenchyma panels show two forms rather than a single fibre in two section directions.

concepts.name: Complex permanent tissue and xylem components
concepts.core_explanation: Book: Complex permanent tissue contains multiple cell types coordinating a common function, especially transport of water, minerals and food, and has two types, xylem and phloem. Xylem comprises tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres: thick-walled tubular tracheids and vessels, many dead when mature, conduct water and minerals vertically; parenchyma stores food and assists sideways water conduction; fibres mainly provide support. Outside clarification: xylem parenchyma is living, so the presence of dead conducting elements does not make the whole tissue exclusively dead.

concepts.name: Phloem components and food transport
concepts.core_explanation: Book: The phloem list includes five cell types—sieve cells, sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibres and phloem parenchyma—and describes sieve tubes as tubular cells with perforated walls. Phloem carries food from leaves to other plant parts, and its cells are living except for phloem fibres. Outside clarification: sieve cells and sieve-tube elements are conducting types associated with different plant groups, so the list is a general inventory rather than a requirement that every phloem sample contain all five.

concepts.name: Recognising xylem and phloem in labelled drawings
concepts.core_explanation: Book figures: In paired xylem and phloem drawings, locate xylem parenchyma, vessels, tracheids and xylem fibres, then phloem parenchyma, companion cells, phloem fibres and sieve tubes. In isolated and grouped views, recognise broad vessel elements and tapering tracheids with pitted walls, and sieve-tube elements with transverse sieve plates beside companion cells bearing a nucleus and associated parenchyma. The plasmodesmata label identifies fine connections between neighbouring phloem cells; leader lines name structures rather than transport directions, and one small tracheid label lacks a clearly described leader.

concepts.name: Xylem versus phloem and their arrangement in a stem
concepts.core_explanation: Book: The six comparison rows contrast root-to-leaf water/mineral transport with leaf-to-growing-part food transport, dead with living cells, thick with thin walls, water-impermeability with permeability to food components, lignin with cellulose, and mechanical strength with its absence. The stem diagram locates epidermis, cortex and pith, with inner xylem, intervening cambium and outer phloem; a red enlargement arrow changes scale, while black arrows show upward xylem flow and downward phloem flow in this drawing. Outside correction: viability and wall composition vary among components, lignin reinforces walls rather than constituting entire cells, xylem conducts water through lumens and permits lateral movement through pits, phloem fibres provide support, and food transport can occur toward different sinks rather than invariably downward.

concepts.name: PYQ: adipose tissue and heat conservation
concepts.core_explanation: Book question, HPAS 2020: Fat below the skin acts as a barrier against (a) loss of heat from our body, (b) loss of essential body nutrients, (c) loss of salts from the body, or (d) entry of harmful microorganisms from the environment. Answer basis: book—the adipose function table specifies heat conservation, supporting (a); distinguish this function from nutrient storage or protection against infection.

concepts.name: Practice: meristem locations
concepts.core_explanation: Book question: Evaluate (1) apical tissue is present at root tips only, (2) lateral tissue is beneath bark, and (3) intercalary tissue is at leaf or internode bases. The continued options are (a) 1 only, (b) 1 and 2, (c) 2 and 3, and (d) all are correct. Answer basis: book—(c), because apical meristem occurs at both root and shoot tips, while statements 2 and 3 match the chapter.

concepts.name: Practice: simple permanent tissues and buoyancy
concepts.core_explanation: Book matching question: (1) parenchyma—large vacuole and food storage, (2) sclerenchyma—in climbers and providing mechanical strength, (3) collenchyma—contains lignin; options are (a) 1 only, (b) 2 only, (c) 1 and 3 only, (d) all incorrect; answer basis: book—(a), with flexible climber support assigned to collenchyma and lignification to sclerenchyma. Book lignin question options are (a) parenchyma, (b) sclerenchyma, (c) collenchyma, (d) none; answer basis: book—(b). Book aquatic-parenchyma buoyancy question options are (a) chlorenchyma, (b) sieve tube, (c) aerenchyma, (d) companion cells; answer basis: book—(c), from buoyancy-producing intercellular air spaces.

concepts.name: Practice: identifying the non-xylem component
concepts.core_explanation: Book question: 'All are parts of xylem except' offers (A) companion cells, (B) tracheid, (C) parenchyma and (D) xylem vessel. Answer basis: book—(A), because companion cells belong to phloem, while tracheids, xylem parenchyma and vessels belong to xylem. The unqualified word 'parenchyma' must be interpreted in the xylem-component context.

concepts.name: Practice: cardiac striation versus voluntary control
concepts.core_explanation: Book question asks which cardiac statement is incorrect: (1) striated, (2) voluntary, (3) has features of both skeletal and visceral tissue; the supplied next-page options are (a) 1 only, (b) 1 and 3, (c) 2 only, (d) all are correct. Answer basis: book—statement 2 is incorrect, so (c) answers the page-13 wording; statement 3 refers to striation shared with skeletal muscle and involuntary control shared with visceral muscle. The supplied continuation describes choosing correct statements instead; if that wording were intended, statements 1 and 3 and option (b) would apply, so retain the wording conflict rather than silently changing the question.

concepts.name: Practice: protective plant covering and leaf gas exchange
concepts.core_explanation: Book questions: The layer described as protecting against water loss and secreting a waxy outer substance has options (a) sclerenchyma, (b) epidermis, (c) parenchyma, (d) suberin; the leaf gas-exchange site has options (a) guard cells, (b) stomata, (c) aerenchyma, (d) chlorenchyma. Answer basis: outside, standard textbook biology—the intended answers are epidermis (b) and stomata (b); the preceding exposition does not explicitly teach the waxy cuticle or stomatal gas-exchange mechanism. Outside explanation: epidermal cells produce a cuticle that reduces water loss, and stomata are pores regulated by guard cells; do not generalise the question's 'thickest layer' phrase, confuse a pore with its guard cells, or treat suberin as a tissue.

concepts.name: Practice: muscle-to-bone attachment
concepts.core_explanation: Book question: 'Muscle is connected to bone via' offers (a) ligament, (b) tendon, (c) cartilage and (d) none. Answer basis: outside, standard textbook biology—(b), tendon; the book locates dense connective tissue in tendons and ligaments but does not explicitly state their different attachment endpoints in the supplied exposition. Outside explanation: tendons transmit muscle pull to bone, ligaments generally connect bone to bone at joints, and cartilage provides supportive or cushioning surfaces rather than the usual muscle-to-bone attachment.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Cell boundaries, organelles and plant–animal cell differences
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Directly needed to distinguish nucleus, cytoplasm, membrane, wall, vacuole and chloroplast, and to interpret living contents, intercellular spaces, multinucleate fibres and extracellular material.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Chromosomes, homologous pairs, chromatids, DNA replication and chromosome sets
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Directly needed for the eleven cell-division comparisons, including nuclear phases, ploidy, crossing over and correction of the chromosome-doubling claim.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Somatic cells, germ cells, gametes and fertilisation
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Directly needed to understand where mitosis and meiosis occur, what their products do and why chromosome-number reduction matters.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Locations and roles of the named human organs, passages and skeleton
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Directly needed for tissue-location lists: skin, gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts, lung air sacs, kidney tubules and urinary passages, glands and ducts, brain and spinal cord, heart, vessels, bones and joints.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Plant organ landmarks and sections
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Directly needed to locate tissues using root and shoot tips, leaf base, node, internode, petiole, bark, vascular bundle, seed coverings, dicot and monocot, and the named stem regions.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Diffusion, absorption, secretion and movement through walls or pores
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Directly needed to interpret thin exchange surfaces, epithelial and gland functions, microvilli, tissue-fluid movement, permeability, wall pits, sieve plates and stomatal gas exchange.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Photosynthesis, food storage and the functions of structural biological materials
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Directly needed to understand chlorophyll and food production, transport from leaves, fat as an energy reserve, and how proteins, polysaccharides, cellulose, lignin, keratin and suberin differ from tissues.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Physical meanings of tension, elasticity, pressure, buoyancy and insulation
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Directly needed to connect fibres with pulling and recoil, muscle contraction with movement or pumping, air spaces with floating, and subcutaneous fat with reduced heat loss; also distinguishes lengthwise growth from increased girth.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Stimulus, nerve impulse, electrical signal and voluntary versus involuntary control
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Directly needed to distinguish muscle-control categories and understand the neuron's directional signal diagram; these meanings cannot be inferred from shape or organ location alone.

Epithelial shape–layer–location–function combinations are high-yield matching material, especially diffusion, protection, secretion and stretching.
Diagrams test recognition independently of memorised names, including apparent versus true stratification.
Matrix, collagen, elastic and reticular fibres distinguish connective tissue and explain mechanical properties.
Locations and functions of cartilage, bone, blood, adipose and dense connective tissue are directly examinable.
Haversian canals, canaliculi, chondrocytes, adipocytes and blood-cell labels are distinctive identification facts.
Three-way muscle comparison tests branching, striation, nuclei, control, location and function; cardiac muscle breaks the striated-equals-voluntary shortcut.
Neuron parts, synapse location and signal direction are central structure–function questions.
The complete plant-tissue hierarchy supports classification and component-based elimination.
Apical, lateral and intercalary locations and length-versus-girth effects are directly tested by a supplied statement question.
Chlorenchyma versus aerenchyma distinguishes photosynthesis from buoyancy and is directly tested.
Living versus dead cells, primary versus lignified secondary walls, spaces, contents, occurrence and support functions are core simple-tissue comparisons.
Four xylem components and their conduction, storage and support functions enable precise odd-one-out answers.
Phloem membership and the dead-fibre exception prevent misleading all-living generalisations.

Supplied questions test epidermis versus wall material and stomatal pore versus guard cells; explanations require clearly marked outside support.
Tendon versus ligament versus cartilage is a high-yield attachment and function distinction directly tested on the page.
